html:
The Nigerian Civil War, or Biafran War, was fought from 1967 to 1970 between the government of Nigeria and the breakaway Republic of Biafra in the mainly Igbo southeast. It ended in Biafra's defeat after a blockade and a famine that killed somewhere between half a million and two million people, most of them from hunger.

In January 1966 a coup led mostly by Igbo officers killed northern leaders. A countercoup in July brought Yakubu Gowon to power, and massacres of Igbo in the north drove many hundreds of thousands east. In May 1967 the eastern governor Odumegwu Ojukwu declared Biafra independent. The east held most of the oil found since Oloibiri in 1956, which raised the stakes. Britain and the Soviet Union armed Nigeria; few states recognised Biafra.

Federal troops took the coast and tightened the blockade. Pictures of starving children set off one of the first great televised relief campaigns. Biafra surrendered in January 1970, and Gowon declared "no victor, no vanquished".

The war marked Nigeria's writers. Chinua Achebe served Biafra abroad; Wole Soyinka was jailed for trying to broker peace; and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie retold it in Half of a Yellow Sun.
